Gulf of Alaska sperm whales

Gulf of Alaska
longline depradation
ForagingSocial

Whales prey on sablefish on longline in Gulf of Alaska, first observed anecdotally in 1970s (Schakner et al. 2014)

Recorded since 1970
Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Whales prey on sablefish on longline in Gulf of Alaska, first observed anecdotally in 1970s (Schakner et al. 2014)

Vertical: suspected unknown

Horizontal: increase in depradation over observed period 1998 to 2010 fits 'Wave of Advance' model of social transmission. "While adult male sperm whales found on high latitude feeding grounds are generally thought to forage solitarily [19], our results also show that groups are more likely to be present during depredation events than solitary animals...Aggregating around prey resources may facilitate social learning and may reveal an underlying male sociality" (Schakner et al. 2014)

Oblique: suspected unknown

Domains: foraging; social

Anthropogenic effects: depradation behavior caused by and interacts with human fishing activity

Sources: [1]

Plus-One clan

off Galápagos Islands and Ecuador
coda dialect
CommunicationSocial

Sperm whales socially communicate with stereotyped click patterns, with vocal clans defined by social units sharing similar coda repertoires. Plus-One clan repertoire characterized by codas with pause before final click.

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Sperm whales socially communicate with stereotyped click patterns, with vocal clans defined by social units sharing similar coda repertoires. Plus-One clan repertoire characterized by codas with pause before final click. "recent work showed that sperm whale clans in both the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans could be computationally distinguished by largely clan-specific “identity codas”, as opposed to “nonidentity codas” made by multiple clans (20)…No single coda type is unique to a single clan, which means that clans occasionally make each other’s identity codas. However, the between-clan analyses suggest that clans make other clans’ identity codas less frequently in areas of higher spatial overlap. Theoretically, this adjustment would improve a whale’s ability to quickly discern whether nearby individuals are from their own clan or not, which could guide decisions about social assortment or avoidance (21, 38). Although sperm whales associate at the surface, over 70% of their time is spent independently foraging (39). Identity coda symbolic markers could help whales reunite and reaffirm their social ties in between long foraging dives, even in the absence of other clans" (Hersh et al. 2022)

Vertical: modeling social transmission with agent-based models informed by sperm whale social structure and acoustic data. "Whereas vertical, mother–offspring, social learning can establish and maintain behavioural traits in some cetacean populations (for example, tool use and foraging tactics in bottlenose dolphins)49,54, our models suggest that oblique social learning is necessary to promote clan-like vocal repertoires among sperm whales." (Cantor et al. 2015)

Horizontal: suspected unknown

Oblique: modeling social transmission with agent-based models informed by sperm whale social structure and acoustic data. "Whereas vertical, mother–offspring, social learning can establish and maintain behavioural traits in some cetacean populations (for example, tool use and foraging tactics in bottlenose dolphins)49,54, our models suggest that oblique social learning is necessary to promote clan-like vocal repertoires among sperm whales." (Cantor et al. 2015)

Domains: communication; social

Regular clan

off Galápagos Islands
coda dialect
CommunicationSocial

Sperm whales socially communicate with stereotyped click patterns, with vocal clans defined by social units sharing similar coda repertoires. Regular clan has nine identity codas with regularly-spaced clicks.

Social unit: Family. "The foundation of sperm whale society is the matrilineally based social unit of ten or so females and their offspring" Social units associate primarily with other social units with shared coda repertoires, termed clans (Whitehead 2024) [4]

Conservation status: Vulnerable (VU)

GBIF: 8123917
